778.title: Fatimah and Ali
778.hook: the Prophet's daughter Fatimah marries Ali, and the bride price is a coat of armor (Abu Dawud)
778.howItsDone: Muslim weddings vary widely by culture, but the mahr given to the bride and a walimah, a wedding meal, are part of the practice, and some couples keep both deliberately modest, remembering Fatimah and Ali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, the day itself: two young men in the row, and a verse that called the Muslims small. Your line was: few against many. Did you thank someone you hadn't expected much from? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

A young man wants to marry, and he has almost nothing. That's Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. The woman is Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In Medina, Ali asks for her hand, and the Prophet asks him: what will you give her? Ali says he has nothing. And the Prophet, who knows him well, asks a very practical question: where is your armor? Not a poem. Not a promise. Today: mahr.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WITH ALMOST NOTHING.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE HER?` → `WHERE IS YOUR ARMOR?`

segments.voice: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Abbas. Ali says he has nothing to give, and the Prophet reminds him of his coat of armor, and that armor becomes the mahr, the bride's gift. In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride, not to her father. So the wedding of the Prophet's own daughter starts with a coat of mail. Another report, in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i, lists what the Prophet gave Fatimah for the new home: a cloth, a water skin, and a leather pillow stuffed with a fragrant grass. That's the whole list. A small house, a few things, and two people. Set beside it the advice the Prophet gave Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when Abd al-Rahman married, the Prophet told him to hold a wedding meal, even if only with one sheep. The meal mattered. The size didn't. And the marriage itself was ordinary in the best sense. Bukhari tells of a day the Prophet came to Fatimah's house and Ali wasn't there. She said there had been something between them, and he had gone out angry. The Prophet found him asleep in the mosque, his cloak slipped off and his side covered in dust. He began brushing the dust off him, saying: get up, Abu Turab. Father of dust. Ali, the report says, loved that name more than any other. A small quarrel, a father-in-law who came with a joke instead of a lecture. In Bukhari too, the Prophet says: Fatimah is a part of me. Sunni and Shi'a tradition both honor Fatimah and Ali, and this is where their household began: with very little, and with love.
screen: `THE MAHR WAS A COAT OF ARMOR.` · `A CLOTH, A WATER SKIN, A PILLOW.` · `A MEAL, EVEN WITH ONE SHEEP.` · `GET UP, ABU TURAB.` · then, large: `A SIMPLE WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep a celebration simple. Sit, and settle your breath. Think of something coming up that you're meant to mark: a birthday, an anniversary, a graduation, a small win at work. Notice what you've been planning, and what it costs, in money and in worry. Now ask what the armor is: the one thing that actually matters in it. A meal together. A word said out loud. The right people in the room. Let the rest fall away for a moment. If you pray, you can ask Allah for blessing on the people you'll celebrate with. If you don't, just hold their faces in mind. The bell holds the time.
Mahr, the bride's gift. Fatimah and Ali married with a coat of armor for hers, and a home of very few things. Today's word.
Your line: a simple wedding. Today, cut one thing from a plan that's grown too big, and keep the meal, the word, or the people. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Uhud: the archers
779.hook: the archers are told not to leave their hill, even if they see birds snatching the army; they leave for the spoils, and the victory turns (3:152; Bukhari)
779.howItsDone: Muslims read the Uhud passage of Surah Al Imran as a lesson in obedience and forgiveness, and the story of the archers is a common theme in sermons and sirah classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahr: a coat of armor for a bride's gift, and a home of very few things. Your line was: a simple wedding. What did you cut from a plan that had grown too big? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Even if you see birds snatching us, don't leave this place until I send for you. That's the order, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in close paraphrase. The Meccans have come back after Badr, to the foot of a mountain outside Medina called Uhud. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ places a company of archers on a small hill, under a companion named Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the army's back. The order couldn't be clearer. Stay. Whatever you see, stay. Today: Uhud.
screen: `EVEN IF YOU SEE BIRDS SNATCHING US.` → `DON'T LEAVE THIS PLACE.` → `UNTIL I SEND FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: At first, the battle goes the Muslims' way. In Bukhari's report, the Meccan line breaks and starts to run. From the hill, the archers can see it: the enemy fleeing, the camp left behind, everything there for the taking. And some of them start calling out: the spoils, the spoils! Your companions have won, what are you waiting for? Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? They answer that they'll go down to the people and take their share. And they go. The hill is left nearly empty, and the battle turns. In the confusion, Muslims are killed, and the Prophet himself is wounded. Surah Al Imran tells this moment without softening it. Allah kept His promise to you, the verse says, when you were driving them back, until your courage failed, and you argued about the order, and you disobeyed, after He had shown you what you longed for. Then a short line that names the whole thing, in Pickthall's words: "Some of you desired the world, and some of you desired the Hereafter." That's the hill and the valley, in one sentence. The verse doesn't name names. It says some, and some, in one army, on one afternoon. And then the verse does something surprising. After all that, it says Allah has forgiven them. In Bukhari's report, the archers thought the job was done: your companions have won, they said, and their share was waiting below. Some Muslim teachers tell Uhud to name a very ordinary temptation: leaving your post a little early, because the reward is right there and the work looks finished.
screen: `THE MECCAN LINE BREAKS.` · `THE SPOILS, THE SPOILS!` · `HAVE YOU FORGOTTEN WHAT HE TOLD YOU?` · `THE WORLD, OR THE HEREAFTER.` · then, large: `STAY ON THE HILL.`

segments.voice: The practice: finish your duty before your share. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one place where you've been asked to hold a post: a child you're watching, a shift you're covering, a promise to a friend, a task someone is counting on. Now notice the pull toward the valley: the phone, the reward, the moment you can call it done before it is. You don't have to fight it. Just see it clearly, the way the archers could see the spoils. Then, in your mind, stay on the hill one breath longer. If you pray, you can ask Allah for steadiness. If you don't, simply rest in the choice. The bell holds the time.
Uhud: the mountain outside Medina where a victory turned, after archers left their hill for the spoils, and the verse that named it and forgave them. Today's word.
Your line: stay on the hill. Today, when something you're responsible for looks finished, give it five more minutes before you go for your share. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Uhud: those who shielded him
780.hook: Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Talhah and Abu Talhah shield the wounded Prophet ﷺ with their bodies, and Fatimah tends his wound (sirah; Bukhari)
780.howItsDone: Muslims retell the defenders of Uhud in sirah lessons and sermons, and Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Umm Umarah, is named as an example of women's courage in the early community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uhud, and the archers who left their post for the spoils. Your line was: stay on the hill. Did you give something five more minutes before you called it done? Day seven hundred eighty.

Same battle, a little later. The hill is empty, the enemy has come around it, and the Muslim lines have broken. People are running. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is hurt, and a rumor goes through the field that he has been killed. Around him, a handful of people do the opposite of running. They close in. One of them came out that morning carrying nothing but a water skin. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, and she is remembered as Umm Umarah. Today: Uhud, and the ones who stood in front.
screen: `THE LINES HAVE BROKEN.` → `A HANDFUL CLOSE IN.` → `SHE CAME OUT CARRYING WATER.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah's story comes to us through the early biographers, in Ibn Ishaq's account. Later, another woman asked her what happened at Uhud, and she told it plainly. She had gone out early with a water skin, to give the fighters a drink. When the Muslims were routed, she went to where the Prophet was, and she fought, with a sword and with a bow, to keep people away from him, until she was wounded herself. The woman who asked her said she saw the scar on her shoulder, deep and hollow. Nusaybah was not the only one. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps two more. A man named Qays says he saw the hand of Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, paralyzed. It was the hand he had held up to shield the Prophet at Uhud. And Anas says that Abu Talhah stood before the Prophet with his shield, a strong archer, and when the Prophet raised his head to look at the enemy, Abu Talhah told him: don't look out, an arrow might hit you. My chest before your chest. Then there's what came after. Bukhari reports that the Prophet's face was cut, his helmet broken on his head, a tooth broken. Fatimah, his daughter, the bride from two days ago, washed the blood from his face while Ali poured water from his shield. When the bleeding wouldn't stop, she burned a piece of a reed mat and pressed the ash into the wound, and it stopped. A water skin, a raised hand, a shield, a handful of ash. Four people, four small things. Each of them stood between him and harm.
screen: `A WATER SKIN, THEN A SWORD AND A BOW.` · `TALHAH'S HAND, PARALYZED.` · `MY CHEST BEFORE YOUR CHEST.` · `FATIMAH AND THE ASH.` · then, large: `SHE STOOD IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand by someone under attack. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's taking blows right now. Maybe online, maybe at work, maybe in their own family, maybe in their own head. Picture them clearly. Then picture yourself stepping a little closer, the way Nusaybah moved toward the Prophet instead of away. You don't need a sword. Ask what your water skin is, what your shield is, what your ash is: a message, a word in a meeting, a meal dropped at the door. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask Allah to protect them. If you don't, just keep them in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Uhud, again: the battle where the lines broke, and Nusaybah, Talhah, Abu Talhah and Fatimah each stood between the Prophet and harm. Today's word.
Your line: she stood in front. Today, do the one thing you chose for the person under attack, before the day is out. Day seven hundred eighty.

781.title: Medina's broken covenants
781.hook: the city's Jewish tribes and the Muslims fall into conflict, with exiles and a hard judgment on Banu Qurayza, which historians still study carefully (Bukhari; 59:2)
781.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and teachers discuss the conflicts with Medina's Jewish tribes in sirah study, through the lens of the charter and its breaking; historians of all backgrounds continue to examine the sources.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uhud, and the people who stood between the Prophet and harm: a water skin, a hand, a shield, and ash. Your line was: she stood in front. Did you do the one thing you chose? Day seven hundred eighty-one.

Some chapters are easy to tell. This one isn't, and it would be dishonest to skip it. A week ago on this path, the charter of Medina named Jewish clans alongside the believers, bound to defend the city together. That hope did not hold. One after another, three Jewish tribes of the city came into conflict with the Muslims. Some were sent into exile. One met a judgment that is hard to read. The Muslim sources record it, and historians still study it carefully. Today we tell it as plainly as we can: ahd.
screen: `BOUND TO DEFEND THE CITY TOGETHER.` → `THAT HOPE DID NOT HOLD.` → `TOLD AS PLAINLY AS WE CAN.`

segments.voice: The Muslim sources tell this as a story about covenants. The Arabic word is ahd, a pledge, a binding promise. The charter bound the groups it names to defend the city together and not to aid its enemies. The three large tribes of this story, Qaynuqa, Nadir and Qurayza, aren't named in it; Ibn Ishaq says each had its own pact with the Prophet. In Ibn Ishaq's biography, the tribe of Qaynuqa breaks with the Muslims, and they leave Medina with their goods. Sahih al-Bukhari, in a report from Ibn Umar, puts the next two side by side. Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza fought the Muslims, he says, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sent Banu Nadir into exile and let Banu Qurayza stay. Surah al-Hashr opens on that exile: people going out from their homes, their strongholds unable to protect them. Later, during a siege of the city, the sources say Banu Qurayza broke their treaty and sided with the armies outside. Afterward they surrendered, and agreed to be judged by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a leader of the Aws, their old allies. Bukhari reports his judgment: their fighting men were to be killed, and their women and children taken captive. The Prophet accepted it. That is in the sources, and it shouldn't be smoothed over. Historians, Muslim and not, have examined these accounts closely. Some question details of the later reports, including the numbers, which vary; others defend them. In the Muslim sources, the judgment is framed as a sentence for breaking a treaty in wartime, not as a ruling on a people or a faith. And the people of that time are not the people of this one. No one listening today, Jewish or Muslim, is on trial for it. What's asked of us is harder and quieter: to know it, and not to look away.
screen: `AHD: A BINDING PROMISE.` · `EXILE: QAYNUQA, THEN NADIR.` · `QURAYZA AND THE JUDGMENT OF SA'D.` · `HISTORIANS STILL WEIGH THE ACCOUNTS.` · then, large: `HARD HISTORY, TOLD HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with a hard history, without anger. Let the breath slow. Bring to mind a painful chapter in a story you belong to: your country's, your family's, your faith's, your own. Don't defend it. Don't attack it. Just let the facts stand there, the way they're written. When anger rises, at them, at us, at whoever, notice it, and let it pass like weather. Remember that everyone in that chapter had a face and a name. If you pray, you can ask Allah for mercy on all who suffered. If you don't, simply hold them in silence. The bell holds the time.
Ahd, a pledge. The charter that made one community, the exiles and the judgment that followed, recorded in the Muslim sources and still studied by historians. Today's word.
Your line: hard history, told honestly. Today, when a painful part of your own story comes up, tell it plainly, without excuses and without blame. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: The Trench
782.hook: Salman's trench, the whole city digging on a cold morning, a rock that breaks, and Jabir's small meal that feeds the diggers (Bukhari)
782.howItsDone: The Battle of the Trench, al-Khandaq, is taught in sirah classes, and the diggers' call and answer from Sahih al-Bukhari is sometimes recited as an example of the Prophet working alongside his companions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahd, the hardest chapter on this stretch of the path. Your line was: hard history, told honestly. Did a painful part of your own story come up, and could you tell it plainly? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A cold morning, and the sound of picks on stony ground. A great army of allied tribes is coming for Medina. The biographers say the plan came from Salman the Persian: dig a trench across the open side of the city. Anas, in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes the scene. The Muhajirun and the Ansar, the people of Mecca and the people of Medina, are digging in the cold, and they have no servants to do it for them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes out and sees how tired and hungry they are. Today: the Trench.
screen: `A COLD MORNING.` → `SALMAN'S PLAN.` → `NO SERVANTS TO DIG FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: What he does first is sing with them. In Anas's report, he calls out a line of verse: O Allah, the real life is the life of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun. And the diggers call back: we are the ones who pledged to Muhammad, to strive as long as we live. A call and an answer, across a ditch. Al-Bara, also in Bukhari, adds that the Prophet carried earth himself until the dust covered his belly, and as he worked he recited the verses of the poet Abdullah ibn Rawahah: without You, O Allah, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed, so send calm down on us and make our feet firm. Firm feet: the same gift as the night rain before Badr. Then the rock. Jabir says they hit a hard rock no one could break, and they went to the Prophet. He came, took the pick, and struck, and the rock fell apart into loose sand. Another report, in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i, tells of three strikes at a rock, each one throwing off a flash of light. And then Jabir tells something smaller and lovelier. Seeing the Prophet's hunger, he slipped home. His wife had a little barley and a young goat, and they cooked it, and Jabir quietly invited the Prophet, with one or two others. Instead the Prophet called out to the whole trench: Jabir has made a meal, come on! Jabir's wife, worried, asked if the Prophet knew how little there was. He did. In Jabir's telling, everyone ate their fill, and the pot was still bubbling. Many hands, one trench, one pot.
screen: `A CALL AND AN ANSWER, ACROSS A DITCH.` · `DUST ON HIS BELLY, FEET MADE FIRM.` · `THE ROCK FALLS INTO SAND.` · `JABIR'S SMALL MEAL FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `DIG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: work beside others. Sit, and breathe. Think of a job ahead of you that's shared: a project at work, cleaning up after a family meal, a neighborhood thing, a group assignment. Notice where you usually stand: in front giving directions, off to the side, or not there at all. Now picture yourself in the ditch with everyone else, carrying a basket of earth. Notice who's tired. Notice who's hungry. Think of one small thing you could bring, like Jabir's pot. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless the work and the people doing it. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Trench: Salman's plan, dug by the people of Mecca and Medina together in the cold, with the Prophet carrying earth and singing beside them. Today's word.
Your line: dig together. Today, do one shared chore you usually leave to others, and do it next to them, not instead of them. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: The wind
783.hook: on a freezing night of the siege, Hudhayfah crosses to the enemy camp, holds his arrow, and the wind scatters the confederate armies (33:9; Muslim)
783.howItsDone: Muslims recite the opening of the Confederates passage, 33:9 onward, as a reminder of rescue under siege, and the phrase hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil is said by some in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trench: a call and an answer across a ditch, and Jabir's small pot that fed everyone. Your line was: dig together. Did you work next to someone, not instead of them? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

Who will go and bring me news of the enemy? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks it of his companions on a bitter night of the siege. The trench has held, but the armies are still camped on the far side, and the siege drags on. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman remembers this night in Sahih Muslim. No one answers. The Prophet asks again. Silence. He asks a third time. Still no one stands up. Today: the wind.
screen: `WHO WILL BRING ME NEWS?` → `A BITTER NIGHT OF THE SIEGE.` → `NO ONE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Then the Prophet calls one man by name: get up, Hudhayfah. And Hudhayfah says that once he was named, he had no choice. The Prophet gives him two instructions. Bring me news of them. And don't stir them up against me. So he goes, alone, across the dark. And here's the strange part of his telling: on the way, he felt as if he were walking in a warm bath. He reaches the enemy camp and sees Abu Sufyan, the Meccan commander, warming his back at a fire. Hudhayfah fits an arrow to his bow. He wants to shoot. He says he would have hit him. And then he remembers: don't stir them up. He lowers the bow. He walks back, still warm, and gives his report, and the moment he's done, the cold comes back. The Prophet wraps him in a spare cloak he used for prayer, and Hudhayfah sleeps there until morning, when the Prophet wakes him: get up, sleeper. Meanwhile, the camp he had walked through was coming apart. Surah al-Ahzab remembers it in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see." The biographers say the wind knocked over pots and blew out fires, and the armies packed up and left. In Bukhari, the Prophet says afterward: now we will go to them, and they will not come to us. Notice what Hudhayfah did not do. The one dramatic act within his reach, he held back. The ending didn't come from his arrow. In the Qur'an's telling, it came from the wind.
screen: `GET UP, HUDHAYFAH.` · `DON'T STIR THEM UP.` · `THE ARROW HELD BACK.` · `A GREAT WIND AND HOSTS YE COULD NOT SEE.` · then, large: `THE WIND CAME.`

segments.voice: The practice: wait out a storm. Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of something you're under siege from right now: a conflict, a worry, a stretch of waiting. Notice the arrow in your hand: the angry email, the sharp word, the move that would feel good for one second and stir everything up. Don't fire it. Just hold it, the way Hudhayfah held his. Notice what it's like to wait instead. If you pray, you can recite "hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil", Allah is enough for us, and the best guardian, the words of 3:173. If you don't, simply rest, and let the storm be the storm. The bell holds the time.
The wind: the great wind of Surah al-Ahzab that broke up the armies around Medina, on the night Hudhayfah held his arrow. Today's word.
Your line: the wind came. Today, when you're tempted to fire off the one thing that would stir things up, hold it, and wait a little longer. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: The pilgrims turned back
784.hook: fourteen hundred set out as pilgrims for Mecca; the Prophet's camel kneels and won't go on, and they are stopped at the well of Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari)
784.howItsDone: Muslims setting out for hajj or umrah enter ihram at set points on the road, as the pilgrims of Hudaybiyyah did, and the story of the journey is taught in sirah classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wind, and Hudhayfah lowering his bow in the enemy camp. Your line was: the wind came. Did you hold back the one thing that would have stirred things up? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

This time they aren't marching to a battle. They're going on pilgrimage. Sahih al-Bukhari describes them setting out from Medina with their sacrificial animals garlanded and marked, and entering the state of ihram, the pilgrim's state, on the road. Al-Bara, who was there, says they were fourteen hundred. The goal is the Ka'bah, the house they have faced in prayer from far away. And then, close to Mecca, the Prophet's camel kneels down in the road and won't get up. Today: the pilgrims turned back.
screen: `NOT A BATTLE: A PILGRIMAGE.` → `ANIMALS GARLANDED, PILGRIMS IN IHRAM.` → `THE CAMEL KNEELS.`

segments.voice: The camel's name is al-Qaswa, and in Bukhari's long report the people around her start saying: al-Qaswa has turned stubborn. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ answers: she hasn't, that isn't her nature. She has been held back by the One who held back the elephant. That's a reference to Surah al-Fil, the army with the elephant that never reached the Ka'bah. A stopped animal, and he reads it as a sign: not this way, not by force. Then he says something that sets the tone for everything that follows: by the One in whose hand is my soul, if they ask me for any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred, I will grant it. He turns the camel and they camp at Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, by a well with very little water. Al-Bara tells what happened there. They drew the well until it was dry. The Prophet came and sat at its edge, asked for some water, rinsed his mouth, made a supplication, and poured it back into the well. After a while, he says, the well gave enough for them and their animals. So here they are: pilgrims in ihram, at the far end of Hudaybiyyah, with water in the well and a closed door ahead. The Meccans will not let them in. What comes next, this path will tell over the coming days: a pledge, a treaty, and an argument over a single word. Today is only the stopping. Look back at this week, and much of it has been about stopping: archers who should have stayed, defenders who held their ground in front, a man who held his arrow. And now a whole caravan, halted at the edge.
screen: `AL-QASWA KNEELS.` · `HELD BACK BY THE ONE WHO HELD BACK THE ELEPHANT.` · `A DRY WELL AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` · `A CLOSED DOOR AHEAD.` · then, large: `STOPPED AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept a closed door. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one door that's closed to you right now: a job that went to someone else, a relationship that won't open back up, a plan the world simply said no to. Picture yourself at its edge, in your best clothes, ready. Don't push on it. Don't kick it. Just let your hand rest on it. Then turn around, and look for the well: what's here, where you are, that you haven't drawn from yet. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you the well. If you don't, rest in the turning. The bell holds the time.
Hudaybiyyah, the well at the edge of the sacred land where the pilgrim caravan, in ihram for the Ka'bah, was stopped. Today's word.
Your line: stopped at the edge. Today, when a door closes, take one breath before you push, and ask what the stop might be for. Day seven hundred eighty-four.
